metadata.title: Circumventing construct-irrelevant variance in international assessments using cognitive diagnostic modeling: A curriculum-sensitive measure

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 1995 mathematics data for secondary students (seventh, eighth, and ninth graders) and restricts the analytic sample to educational systems with at least 60% valid teacher-level information and to students with non-missing teacher data for the DINA model. The authors explicitly state that sampling weights were used to calculate country means for the Tc and IRT-based scores, and that all five plausible values were used for the IRT-based means. For the Tc statistic, the country-wise Tc is computed from MG-DINA posterior skill probabilities combined with teacher-reported topic coverage at the classroom level; the paper does not report a specific weight variable name, but it indicates complex-sample weighting at the country-mean stage. Replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not described, so uncertainty estimation at the replicate level is not extractable from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The target population is 13-year-old secondary school students (seventh, eighth, and ninth graders) in TIMSS 1995 mathematics. Of 45 educational systems participating, the authors include only those with at least 60% valid teacher-level information at the classroom level, yielding 19 relevant countries/systems and 142,077 students initially. They then exclude students with missing teacher data required for the DINA/MG-DINA estimation, reducing the effective sample size to 56,525 students. To meet the conditional independence assumption for MG-DINA as strictly as possible, they further exclude students who did not answer more than 20 questions (230 students, 0.09% of the full sample). For the CDM, they code partial credit items as correct only when the maximum points were obtained, code unanswered items as wrong, and treat booklet-missing items due to design as missing (not considered in person ability estimation).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study proposes a curriculum-sensitive scaling statistic, Tc, within cognitive diagnostic modeling (CDM) to address construct-irrelevant variance in international assessments when teachers do not cover all tested topics. The empirical demonstration uses TIMSS 1995 mathematics data for secondary students (seventh–ninth graders) across 19 educational systems/countries, combining student item responses with teacher survey reports of which of 32 math topics were taught in class. The authors estimate an MG-DINA model (with an 11-skill Q-matrix) and compute Tc as the average proportion of taught topics that students did not master, then rank countries by Tc (ascending). For comparison, they compute conventional IRT-based country means using sampling weights and all five plausible values. The resulting Tc ranking is highly consistent with the official IRT-based ranking (country-mean correlation r = −0.95; full-sample vs reduced-sample IRT correlation r = 0.99), with only two countries differing by more than one rank. Limitations include substantial missing teacher information requiring sample reduction and potential mismatch between teacher questionnaire topics and the test’s skill/Q-matrix structure. data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses cognitive diagnostic modeling (MG-DINA) and compares rankings, it does not train a supervised ML predictive model with a specified target variable and reported predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE). The extraction therefore leaves ml_techniques and main_findings empty because the study’s core contribution is a new measurement/scaling statistic and ranking comparison rather than an ML prediction task. The provided text also does not report per-country sample sizes in a way that can be extracted into n_students for each analyzed economy.
